This game is fantastic at its core, but I cannot recommend it in its current state.

This game was marketed as both a PVP and PVE experience, yet the reality is that the PVE side has been almost completely erased by the way the community and loadout system function. The overwhelming majority of players have adopted the kill-on-sight or worse, the befriend and betray mentality, which wouldn't necessarily be a problem if the risk and reward were balanced.

Right now, there is little to no incentive to bring high-tier gear into a raid. Any player can load into a game with a free loadout and still reliably kill someone who is risking valuable gear. This creates a situation where hoarding gear isn't just encouraged, but required, because bringing anything good almost guarantees you'll lose it to someone with nothing to lose.

As a result, the PVE content suffers immensely. ARCS are actively avoided because engaging them requires gear that is too risky to bring. This problem is even worse for new or casual players, because they cannot acquire and retain the gear needed to take down bigger ARCS. This means a lot of quests cannot be fulfilled unless you are blessed with a kind lobby, or you simply join the rats and steal from others. The PVE aspect essentially becomes useless then, and you are left in a frustrating loop where ignoring half of the advertised experience is the only way to progress.

The longer this continues, the worse this problem will become. As the weeks go by and the player base becomes more established, new and casual players will have an increasingly difficult time acquiring the materials needed to upgrade their workstations. Without upgraded workstations, they cannot craft better gear, meaning they cannot engage with PVE content, which is required for the majority of quests. This leaves them effectively stuck at the start of the game.

The aggression-based matchmaking does little to alleviate the loadout problem, because in most matches, there are still multiple highly aggressive players who camp the spawn and extraction zones and kill Raiders, again risking little on their part. Some of these spawn camp deaths also occur while the players load in, as mid-game spawns are enabled and poorly protected from trolls.

If this game were marketed as a PVP extraction shooter or a PVE co-op game, there would be no problem with either playstyle. However, the current blend of both creates an unfun, toxic and exhausting loop full of childish people who cannot work cooperatively and who believe that shooting people in the back while risking none of their own gear is the only way to enjoy the game. And any attempt to raise these concerns is routinely dismissed as a skill issue on the new player's part, despite the fact that the game actively rewards low-risk griefing over meaningful cooperation or PVE battles.

TLDR - ARC Raiders is supposed to be a blend of PVP and PVE, but its current systems reward zero-risk PVP with free loadouts while punishing anyone engaging with PVE. This makes progression nearly impossible for new and casual players, and any criticism is brushed off by the community as a 'skill issue', despite the issue being rooted in the poor balance and design.

I went in thinking:
“Oh cool, another battle royale.”
Buys game. Loads in.
Wait… this is definitely not that.
(Poor research was done on my behalf.)

Turns out it’s an AI-robots-taking-over-the-world extraction shooter, with loot decided by RNGesus himself. And honestly? I liked it. Loved it, even. Butterflies. Real ones. The kind that steal your lunch money later.

First few games:
Community says, “Hey Raider, don’t shoot.”
Wow. A friendly community? In this economy?
We loot together. We vibe. We emote. We believe in humanity.

Then it hits me.

Friendly lobbies are actually the worst thing ever invented.

Why? Because we’re sharing loot spawns. That shiny, delicious, good good goop is now split between us like a sad pizza. Progress slows. Frustration rises. Monkey brain activates.

So I hit a guy with my stick (Raider tool) because it is not my loot anymore, it is OUR loot. 

Suddenly I’m in a whole new world.

“Don’t shoot” now translates to:
“I will wait for you to loot this container so I can shoot you in the ass.”

Now I can’t PvP (Because I suck).
I can’t loot.
I get 0 items and 100 emotional damage.

Do I stay friendly?
Do I betray first?
Do I want loot or inner peace?

This game is not an extraction shooter — it’s a philosophical experiment.

And let’s talk about the Arc robots.
Because apparently ARC robots — especially Rocketeers — are esports professionals.
They never miss.
They predict my movement.
They predict my misclicks.
I panic, run the wrong direction, and the Rocketeer already knew I would do that before I was born.

It kills me, then hovers there…
watching me…
menacingly…
after destroying both my character and my ego.

After 200 hours, here’s my verdict:

Arc Raiders is a good game.
It is fun.
It is unique.
It is absolutely worth the mental torture.

10/10 — would trust strangers again and get shot in the ass.

Absolutely nailed the environment and atmosphere. Can easily play solo or with a squad and still enjoy it the same. Feels like something we could have got from the last of us 2 multiplayer in terms of atmosphere. Graphics are pristine, performance has been smooth for me since day  1.

Personally this was my game of the year for 2025. Gunplay and PVP feels good if that is your thing, teaming up and doing PVE feels good if you prefer. I think it's really cool that you get more casual friendly lobbies depending on how you play, and I'll often oscillate between these lobbies and the more PVP focused queues depending on how I feel that night.

The only real complaints I've heard is about some of the gun balancing, but pretty much everything feels viable if you play around what you have, however I concede that some of the higher rarity weapons don't feel as rewarding to use when the cost to build and repair them is taken into consideration.

The graphics and overall aesthetic of the game are what pulled me in, and hundreds of hours later I still constantly stop while moving around topside to take in the scenery, it truly is a beautiful game. The two things that kept me around were the high intensity and rewarding social environments the game creates as well the feeling you get when you get out of a successful raid and contribute to whatever goal you were working towards at that point.

The only bad thing I can personally say about the game is that if you sink ungodly amounts of hours into it you will get to a point where there isn't many goals the game puts in front of you anymore. However, that's not really the game's fault, most people won't play that much and, and even if you do, I can appreciate the almost sandbox-like feeling you can get from loading into raids just for the love of the game, after you've already done all the quests, upgraded all of your benches, and fully funded your expedition.

I've already made some great memories in the game, and I'm eager to continue to do so as Embark rolls out more content.

The only major problem I can honestly say I have? Is the glitching during gameplay. It doesn't happen always, but when it does. For example, one game I literally couldn't turn to my right. That's impossible to enjoy during gameplay. Now you have plenty of douchebags who play this but that's with every game. This is definitely a classic that will be around for a long time. Great game!

ARC Raiders can be best described as the shopping-cart litmus test of multiplayer shooters. Your objective is simple: go in, get loot, and leave alive. How you go about doing this exactly is up to you.

To say that you see a target, a full magazine in your hand, and make the assumption that you should shoot at it is incredibly reductive. Everything is a choice. What you decide to take home, what people or ARC you choose to engage, whom to drop some loot for, and which person to side with in a fight you walked into. You are the judge, jury, and in some cases, executioner. You don't even have to go into a raid with a gun. This game will bring the best of the good and the worst of the bad. There will be rats cosplaying as high-tier players with the ill-gotten gains of the slain. There will be raiders that simply pass you by, guns at the ready but not yet pointed at you. If you're lucky, you might be saved by an angel on the grounds, coming to revive a complete stranger in the nick of time. You will get to see the entire moral spectrum on display, and I think that is actually the best quality of this game. Everything else is just a setup that enables the wide variety of experiences you will encounter. 

The game, however, is not apathetic in its matchmaking. This allows a certain degree of control in getting the sort of rounds one would like to partake in. The more hostile one remains, the more hostile the type of servers one will be placed in, and vice versa. This prevents the game from devolving into a race to the bottom that reinforces aggression and a first-strike mentality at all times. This also extends to the solo, duo, and trio queues, the latter of which increase drastically in hostility and with solos being generally non-hostile.

ARC Raiders is not an extraction shooter. It's a psychological thriller that looks like an extraction shooter.

We need to stop acting like everything is okay. The game is fun. The combat is intense the progression is just fast enough. The sound oh the sounds are amazing. The maps are beautiful, it runs well while looking as good if not better than all the games that don't run well. But, the AI voices. Before I continue I want to say that I want to put forth solutions where I can to solve any issues I have with the game. There is one issue I have that I'm not as sure how to solve but we'll get there when we get there.

The first time you hear them, they are good enough that you might not realize or just right it off as a weird choice. Then you hear it again, and again, and again, and never in a way that makes sense to be better than hiring a voice actor. In the Finals I could get over it, they used the tools in interesting ways that would've been almost if not impossible without the technology. Reading people names and calling out specific things that happened, it was actually kind of cool. In Arc Raiders it's just 'Hey look over there' and scripted cutscenes after completing missions, all things done by every other game while not needing AI voices that sounds really bad. As stated they are passible the first few times you hear them, then you hear the same 4 voice lines again and again and notice all the weird details. Pacing, intonation, undefined accents or changing accents. I have tried to turn them off but the NPC voices are tied to the same audio settings as the voices for other players, so if you turn one off the other one turns off as well. You can't just turn them off when you go talk to them because they also talk at the start of a mission so you'd take a minute out of every run to turn the volume back up, and back down at the end before you talk to the NPCs. it's doable but annoying. The solution? Hire voice actors, hopefully the same one's you used to train the AI. Just hire them back and record the lines and replace them. Pretty easy.

Then I saw that they have a mode so you can change your voice for talking to players, at first I thought that was cool, it allows people who might be to scared or shy to participate in the game fully, but I've sense changed my mind for a simple reason. Filters. For long long before we had AI humans have been changing how their voice sounds digitally and to extreme variation. No, I'm not saying everyone should sound like Daft Punk (that'd be funny though) but think of it like this, the input is a regular voice and some filters and modulation they are able to make their voices sound like. That which means every sound from a regular voice to those voices and ones past it are all doable without AI. Picture a world where instead of giving us an AI voice that sounds robotic and X pitches, you got a bunch of sliders that could change how your voice sounded. Pitch your voice up or down, filter it like it's coming through a gas mask or radio, make it so you always talk in perfect pitch, that is all doable without AI and it gives people so much more control, hell I don't have a problem with using my real voice but I'd use it, that sounds cool.

Now those are my actual issues, these next ones are maybe gripes. They aren't deal breakers but are more so annoying when I hear them being talked about. I should say now that I have a degree in computational Physics so I have a background in physics, computer science and understand AI. I'm going to mention it again later but this is the argument I know has holes that I just don't know about, please, inform me.

There other main use of AI is trickier to degrade and I'll be up front with that. It's cool seeing the robots react to our shots and watch them rebalance now that an engine or leg is gone. Embark has come forward and even said that the animations the AI makes are then altered by a human artist to make it look better, better. They look like AI, specifically the Arc with legs. They have this movement to them where it's like the AI found a loophole in how the center of gravity was being calculated so actually the best thing to do is tuck it's leg completely under itself and spin to trick the engine, it looks silly and makes Arc that should be scary look stupid. The issue is, I don't know how you make it better. Maybe there isn't a great alternative, let me know. Right now, The smaller the legs the sillier they look.

The flying Arc look much better but did they need to be powered by AI? I don't think so. Now, I'm not an expert on the subject, I'm not an expert on any of these subjects but this is the one where I believe I could definitely be the most wrong so please tell me, comments are on. In college I was a part of a Quadcopter project and as a part of it we had to program our quadcopter to fly. In that programing, we had to insert *cough**cough* copy and paste *cough**cough* code that would take in the info from the gyroscope on the quadcopter and adjust the engine to automatically stabilize. An arduino could do that in a real life scenario where there are many more variables, possible problems and much less control of what the quadcopter would face. I think a massive server with the hardware to supposedly run an AI model could do this as well. As for them patrolling and finding you, look at every game ever, look at FEAR enemies, the things the Arc are doing are not all that new, just being done differently and sold well. Now for how the flying Arc would work, you have two things going on at the same time, one, a balancing module changing the output of each engine to follow the path that model two makes by taking into account all the completely static things in the world and the player/s if there even is/are one/s. Oh but a stabilizing algorithm couldn't handle an engine being completely gone. If it's possible there is one out there that could figure it out, also, based on how the Arc move after you shoot one of their jets off, I think what is actually happening is that the output of that jet get's lowered significantly but isn't gone. This allows the Arc to still have some amount of balance otherwise it would be impossible.

To end this, I love this game. I bought this game I continue to play it and probably will play it much more in the weeks to come. The thing stopping me from recommending it to people it the AI, the voices most of all. Solo's are full of really great people who are often down to help one another. I can't tell you how many times I've been downed in solo's only for another player to defib me while expecting nothing in return cause the fact that they saved someone that they didn't have to save is enough to make you feel like a hero. Trios can be a bloodbath, but sometimes you'll have 1 guy playing a flute with 3 full teams following him around dancing before everyone extracts together in harmony while cracking jokes in proximity chat.

Sometimes someone will ask you to team up, then kill you once you're looting. Sometimes you make a friend, only to never see them again, yet you'll remember that experience with them because it was a moment you and a stranger came together to do something cool, hectic, or crazy. Sometimes someone will kill you, only to say sorry and get you back up once they realized you weren't much of a threat.

What I love is that this game makes you think. It makes you consider human nature and puts you in a place to be able to come together, or realize you can't trust someone else as much as you thought, and it feels real.

The game does have some flaws, but overall, it's a really fun experience. Arc enemies are challenging, and even the weakest, smallest robots can easily overwhelm you if you're not careful. The larger Arc robots can be terrifying, especially if encountered alone. I don't think there is a single moment in my gaming lifetime that made me sh*t my pants the way I did the first time a Leaper jumped 200m right onto my face.

The aggression-based matchmaking is great because it pairs people up who have similar playstyles, which overall creates a better experience for those who like active PvP, and those who want to PvP situationally based on the potential gain or loss from it. From what I can tell, the only people who hate it are the people who want to be bullies and get satisfaction from shutting someone else's good time down. These people tend to be aggressive PvP'ers wishing they could go against people who won't fight back so they can get free loot, and that doesn't sound fun to me. People who go out of their way to kill people get their comeuppance from others looking to do the same. This is truly a game of karma, where you get back what you put out into the world, and honestly I think that's beautiful.

My biggest 3 issues with this game are:
1. Lack of teaming options - why do I have to queue solo or trio? Why can I not queue for duos with a random stranger?
2. Stash size limitations are extremely frustrating as a new player, especially when you don't know what items to keep, recycle, or sell. 
3. Quests have no map markers, and when you get to an area you have to search around for *something* to interact with, usually without a description of what that thing is.

My favorite 3 things about this game:
1. The community - it's honestly so good. I've had so many good experiences with random people that I'll probably never see again.
2. The movement and combat feels great.
3. The PvE elements are challenging and fun. They hit a homerun on the PvE side of things.

Lastly, please for the love of god fix the bug that doesn't show you your teammates health bars/location. It can be fixed by taking damage and which refreshes the HUD state on that teammate, but it's annoying to have to encounter at all in the first place.

If you are looking for a fun social FPS experience, this game is it.

This isn’t an extraction shooter – it’s just a shooter. Why? The current matchmaking splits players into two camps: "carebears" and PvP "sweats." The first group is basically a Teletubby-style trash-collecting simulator. Players run around, wave at each other, and have dance parties in the extraction elevator, while the ARC machines pose zero threat. There’s no risk, no tension – which is the polar opposite of what this genre is supposed to be.

In the second group, you’re just playing a deathmatch. Players couldn’t care less about loot, progression, or extraction – it’s a pure slugfest to see who can rack up the most kills. There’s absolutely zero "extraction shooter" DNA in that experience.

What’s missing is the middle ground – mixed lobbies where you never know what to expect. There’s no tension because you never have those emergent moments: one minute getting shot in the back by a traitor for your loot, and the next finding a random ally to help you take down a tough ARC. That unpredictability is exactly what should be driving the excitement, but in the current state of the game, it’s non-existent.

I really hope Embark is actually playing their own game and realizes that, in its current state, Arc Raiders isn't what they intended it to be. Then again, after selling 12 million copies, they could just as easily stop caring about development, pack their bags, and move to Hawaii.

The game is still young and new content is on the way – we’ll see if they can actually make something out of this.

Not really a problem if you don't play PvP, or simply don't crave being the largest, most geared person/group on the server... But it even makes playing PvE annoying as you can't even perform basic functions of the game like organizing your inventory when the game is lagging like this. Hopefully the frequency of these issues will decrease as time goes on; seems to be related to all the outages online generally lately so it might not be the fault of Facepunch or those associated.

However when the game works (outside of the usual jankiness that comes with a game from 2013 being updated to 2026) and you're not running into hackers; the game really is fun. Almost addicting even as you'll quickly be consumed by 'scrap addiction' and 'raid paranoia'. Being bound to hit just one more barrel for a morsel of scrap metal, or incessantly checking your base and your hard earned valuables whenever possible like a schizophrenic to prevent an 'offline' attack... Or yk chill playing on a PvE server with optional PvP. A whole different vibe from purist PvP; but a valid way to play as well, especially when the servers are laggin like hell. 

TLDR: So long as you have some friends, don't mind making friends or playing alone; this game is great. But mileage may vary based on what server you're on and the size of your group. Solos inherently have a disadvantage on servers that allow groups, so you'll have to adjust accordingly.

FC 26 is a bold experiment in redefining what football means. 

Passing is optional and completely broken. You press pass, something happens, and you’re left to interpret the result like modern art. Was that a through ball? A clearance? A quiet cry for help from the physics engine? Hard to say, but it’s rarely accurate, and never what you intended. 

Your players actively avoid useful positions. There’s something almost artistic about watching them hide behind defenders or sprint into the same five square meters like it’s a team-building exercise. To be fair, this does add a certain difficulty curve. Just not the fun kind. On a casual level, it’s less "pick up and play" and more “pick up and question your life choices.” You’re not battling the opponent so much as negotiating with your own team, hoping that at least two of them will behave like professional footballers for a few seconds in a row. 

Overall, FC 26 is perfect if you enjoy unpredictability, chaos, and shouting “why are you THERE?” at your screen. If you’re looking for responsive passing, intelligent positioning, or anything resembling tactical awareness, consider it an opportunity to practice patience instead. Lots and lots of patience.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is easily one of the best RPGs I’ve ever played. If you enjoy turn-based combat and anything Dungeons & Dragons–based, this game is an absolute must.

The turn-based system feels incredibly rewarding and strategic without being overwhelming. Every fight feels like a puzzle, and your choices—both in combat and dialogue—actually matter. It genuinely feels like playing a D&D campaign where the dice are always rolling behind the scenes.

The story is rich, emotional, and deeply immersive. Your decisions shape the world, your companions, and even who you become by the end of the game. Speaking of companions—each one is well-written, complex, and memorable. They don’t feel like NPCs; they feel like real party members with their own motives, flaws, and growth.

What really sets Baldur’s Gate 3 apart is the freedom. There’s no single “right” way to play. You can solve problems creatively, fail forward, embrace chaos, or play things safe—and the game adapts to you. It rewards curiosity and experimentation in a way very few games do.

I would highly recommend Baldur’s Gate 3 to anyone who:
- Loves turn-based combat
- Enjoys D&D or tabletop-style storytelling
- Wants a game where choices truly matter
- Likes deep character development and branching narratives

TL;DR:
Unoriginal, exhausting, and frustrating by design. Path of Exile 2 mistakes annoyance for difficulty. Stay away.

Long version:

Path of Exile 2 desperately wants to be “Isometric Dark Souls,” but it completely misses the most important ingredient: rhythm.

Boss fights are a nonstop barrage of AoE spam and overtuned movesets. There are no clever mechanics, no memorable patterns to learn—just more overlapping AoEs, smaller arenas, and bigger damage numbers. Every encounter feels the same, only louder and more punishing. Add to that bosses with absurdly inflated HP pools, and fights turn into tedious endurance tests rather than engaging challenges.

Get ready to spend 10–15 minutes dodging and weaving, landing a single attack whenever the game allows it… only to die in less than one second because you made one mistake or the screen filled with effects. It’s not tense. It’s not satisfying. It’s exhausting.

Progression is nearly nonexistent. Leveling up feels pointless when your reward is “3% something” or “5% something else.” In the later stages, it can take days of grinding just to gain a single level. Maybe you’ll get a useful skill gem along the way—if you’re lucky. More often than not, you won’t.

The lore doesn’t help either. Who is the Beast? Why should I care? Why does every character feel like a variation of the same warlock fantasy? Ascendancy classes aren’t earned through mastery or meaningful challenges, but through poorly designed “Djinn” trials that feel more like punishment than progression.

Those trials deserve special mention. First, you grind a token just to attempt them. Then you’re thrown into a gauntlet of misery where your build barely matters. Tank? Maxed shields? Doesn’t matter. A new mechanic drains a special currency every time you get hit, regardless of whether you actually take damage. Lose it all and it’s over. Back to grinding another token. Dodge 30 times, attack once, repeat. Fun is not part of the equation.

On a technical level, the game is riddled with bugs and performance issues. Frame drops, stutters, visual clutter—you name it. But somehow, the microtransaction shop works flawlessly. It even has its own shortcut key. Priorities, I guess.

After just one hour of playing, I don’t feel excited or challenged. I feel tired.

Path of Exile 2 has a “right” way to play, and that way is abandoning your own idea of fun, grinding endlessly, and eventually copying a popular build from the internet. If that sounds appealing to you, maybe this game is for you. If not, do yourself a favor and stay far away.

The current system is a total loss for the player experience. Being kicked from a full game and thrown into an empty lobby populated by bots is a huge turn-off. When I play multiplayer, I want PvP. Battlefield 6 feels like a real step back in the right direction for the series. The gunplay is tight and satisfying, movement is smooth, and the large-scale battles finally capture that classic Battlefield chaos again. Vehicles feel powerful without completely dominating every match, and when everything clicks, those big cinematic moments happen naturally — the kind Battlefield is known for.

Destruction is better than recent entries, though I still wish more structures were fully destructible instead of just partially reactive.

Performance has been solid for me, and it runs way better than Battlefield 2042 did at launch, which is a huge plus. There are still some bugs and balance issues that need tuning, especially with a few weapons and gadgets, but nothing that completely ruins the experience.

Overall, Battlefield 6 isn’t perfect, but it’s fun, fast, and actually feels like Battlefield again. This game has many of the positive aspects of a Bethesda game.  Immersive first-person view, good voice-overs, and NPCs that have reactions based on choices you've made and things you've accomplished.

Sadly, it also has numerous negatives that take away from that immersion and make it feel like too much of a grind to maintain enjoyment.  Those negatives include:

👎 Inventory management:  I swear I spend more time encumbered or trying to figure out which resources to keep and which resources to sell.  Fallout 4's unlimited storage in a settlement's workbench was much better.

👎 Item interaction:  Per past Bethesda games, picking up anything and everything and finding a use for it is encouraged.  In this game, the Miscellaneous items are either decorations or vendor fodder.  These items are *EVERYWHERE* and in a game where you can manufacture all sorts of stuff, you cannot break these items down into components.

👎 Crafting:  Gated by skill points AND limited resources, crafting is uninteresting and yet another grind.  You can replace mods on items, but the prior mod is lost.

👎 Space suits, Helmets, Packs, Outfits, and hazards:  My end goal would be to have a set of equipment that lets me safely visit any or all destinations without having to constantly swap equipment to match the destination.  Firstly, the current implementation contributes to the inventory management and crafting issues.  Second, it means I can never just stick with the gear that has the visual aesthetic I want.

👎 Outpost linking:  Instead of having one landing pad per outpost that handles traffic for incoming and outgoing resources, you have to have a pair of landing pads per link (one at each end) and they're dedicated to that one link.  Once again, Fallout 4 had a better idea by allowing you to assign a settler to establish a link between settlements.  This should have been easily converted to Starfield with ships, crew, or a combination thereof.  In fact, it would encourage collecting ships and hiring more crew.  If things needed to be more complex, defining a ship's routes to different outposts would have been a possibility.

👎 Container linking bugs:  A cursory search online will show that there's a well-known bug involving linking storage containers and those links breaking if a player manually places any items in one.  The "fix" is to delete and re-establish the link, which when you have rows and columns of containers that are snapped together, is nigh impossible.

👎 Outpost object placement:  Specifically, rotation.  It's horrid!  The recommendation I've read is to use a controller for finer control, but I'm a keyboard and mouse player so that's not acceptable.  Object snapping is very limited and it's so difficult to place things neatly aligned.

All these negatives make the game feel like a complete and utter GRIND.  I have hundreds of hours in Fallout 4, largely because I enjoyed building out each and every settlement.  I have hundreds of hours in Satisfactory because I enjoyed building out sensible logistics.  Neither felt like a grind the way that Starfield does.

The most frustrating thing about this game is that it could have been great. But it's such a miserable slog that it's just not worth it. Buggy quests, locations, and terrain. Obtuse interface with no mini-map, requiring you to constantly pause and bring up the full map, even when blasting along at full speed on the bike. 
The bike controls are awful, too; good luck avoiding terrain or hitting anything during the many speeder-focused missions. Don't worry; the starship controls also suck, with tiny or no indicators for cooldowns, target locations, or orientation (and again, no mini-map, so you're still constantly pausing).
Most major missions are on rails, and simply walking a few feet to the wrong direction brings up a full-screen "RETURN TO GAME" warning with an absurd 10-second countdown; so much for immersion. 
The gameplay loop is infuriating. The game can't decide if it wants to be a stealth game, assassin game, or action game, so it just does all three poorly. There's little to no indication of whether stunning someone (which actually kills them, by the way) will immediately summon every enemy in the area. The enemy detection is worthless. There's no way to survey an area before entering, so for stealth, you're stuck with blind luck or reloading a save once you have a full count of enemies. You can't move or hide bodies, so the first time you assassinate (oh, sorry "permanently knock out") someone, it starts a timer as to when someone will see the body and trigger an alarm. Unlike pretty much every other stealth/assassin game out there, whistling doesn't bring one guard over; it brings literally everyone in earshot, and the moment any of them see you, again, the WHOLE PLACE goes active. That would be fine if this was a functional action game, but your weapon choices are boring, and every useful weapon is gated by the game's idiotic pick-up system that disallows reloading or storing weapons you've found, making every firefight just the same repetitive pew-pew with your little peashooter. Given that these stealth quests make up most of the game's "action," the frustrating and drawn-out gameplay loop is a constant source of misery. 
I played all the way through, in the hope that the decent story and characters would lead to a fun payoff, but no, the endgame is a complete letdown, too. The end "boss" is just a bunch of running and whistling combined with instant death and constant reloads. The best DLC isn't playable until after the main story, so you don't get the most useful upgrades and gear until there's nothing left to do in the game except rep missions (which you don't need because the game's over) and shipping quests (which are pointless because, again, the game is over). 
If you're a huge Star Wars fan, I recommend just reading the storyline on Wookieepedia or watching some videos, Don't slog through this mess like I did, hoping for something good at the end.
